messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
Keanu, a 56-year-old detective of Oceanic descent, carried the weight of a childhood trauma that had shaped the very fabric of his existence. As a young boy, he had endured a period of severe physical abuse at the hands of a caregiver. He remembered one particularly terrifying evening with vivid, visceral clarity: his uncle, in a fit of rage, had cornered him in the small kitchen, his thick, scratchy flannel shirt brushing against Keanu’s face as the blows rained down. All the while, a pot on the stove, forgotten in the chaos, began to burn, filling the air with a choking, acrid stench that became inextricably linked to fear and pain.

For decades, the memory of that night lay dormant, yet its tendrils reached into Keanu’s present. Now, any burnt smell – a forgotten toast in the breakroom at the precinct, smoke from a distant backyard fire pit – could instantly transport him back, flooding him with the full, overwhelming terror of the original event. These moments struck without warning, leaving him momentarily paralyzed, his heart hammering against his ribs, his breath catching in his throat. When he tried to articulate these experiences, to explain the profound impact of the past, he found himself losing the thread, words failing him, unable to form a coherent narrative. What surfaced instead was an intense, white-hot rage, a fury directed at the memory itself, at the injustice, at the powerlessness he felt.

His work as a detective, ironically, intensified these internal battles. Interviewing victims, especially those who were vulnerable or appeared helpless, became a minefield. He found himself avoiding eye contact, keeping his distance, the similarity of their plight to his own childhood experience triggering a deep unease. He had come to believe that his reactions showed him to be a lousy coper, a weakness that gnawed at his self-esteem. He was certain that the event had happened to him because of the sort of person he was, a deeply ingrained conviction that eroded his sense of worth.

Keanu had developed a complex array of strategies to manage the constant threat he perceived. He meticulously avoided wearing any clothes that felt similar in texture or cut to the scratchy flannel shirt his uncle had worn, a small but rigid personal rule that guided his wardrobe choices. When a memory threatened to surface, or when he felt himself getting too close to someone, he would mentally detach, pulling back into himself, creating a protective barrier between his inner world and the external one. This strategy, while offering momentary relief, had gradually isolated him. He found himself avoiding other people altogether, retreating into his own space, both at work and in his personal life. This pervasive avoidance had undoubtedly played a role in the dissolution of his marriage years prior, leaving him increasingly alone.

Sleep offered little respite. He found it incredibly difficult to fall asleep, needing to stay alert, his mind racing through potential threats, his senses heightened to every creak of the floorboards, every distant siren. This constant state of hypervigilance bled into his waking hours; he was perpetually watchful, on guard, scanning his surroundings for danger, his body often reacting with strong physical responses – a sudden jolt, a surge of adrenaline – whenever something reminded him, however subtly, of the stressful experiences of his past. Even positive emotions became confusing, tinged with a strange anxiety, as if happiness itself was a deceptive prelude to pain. His beliefs about how the world worked, about its inherent safety and predictability, had been completely shattered, replaced by a pervasive sense of dread and mistrust.

The cumulative toll of this constant internal battle had become unbearable. The exhaustion, the isolation, the gnawing self-blame – all of it had reached a breaking point. Keanu finally decided to seek help, driven by a deep longing for peace and a quiet fear that if he continued down this path, he would lose himself entirely to the shadows of his past, forever trapped in a world where safety was an illusion and happiness a dangerous trick.
